Gynecology and urology · published research

Varicocectomy-related orchialgia

One randomized trial found lower short-term pain and higher sexual satisfaction after red or near-infrared laser for post-varicocelectomy orchialgia.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One randomized trial found lower short-term pain and higher sexual satisfaction after red or near-infrared laser for post-varicocelectomy orchialgia.

Summary of the Evidence

One 60-participant randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial directly examined persistent orchialgia after varicocelectomy. The study randomized 20 men each to red laser, near-infrared laser, or sham. It is a separate cohort from the chronic testicular-pain trial in the previous row, although both papers came from the same Iranian research group. No animal or in-vitro study of post-varicocelectomy pain was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

Compared with sham, both active-light groups had lower pain scores and higher sexual-satisfaction scores at the trial’s reported follow-up. These are patient-reported outcomes in a defined postoperative group; the article did not establish effects on recurrence beyond the short follow-up or on broader urinary and reproductive outcomes (Momenzadeh et al. 2024).

Animal evidence

No animal model directly examining pain after varicocelectomy was identified. Testicular-injury animal studies were not counted as postoperative-pain evidence.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell or tissue study directly examined post-varicocelectomy orchialgia.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The trial compared 650-nm red visible light at 50 mW and 820-nm near-infrared light at 100 mW with sham. A contact probe was applied bilaterally near the upper scrotal nerve for 15 minutes, three times weekly, over 12 sessions. The paper reports a daily fluence range of 6–25 J/cm². The two active groups changed wavelength and power together, so their results do not establish which wavelength or dose is preferable.

Interpretation

The trial found short-term pain and sexual-satisfaction improvements versus sham after varicocelectomy. This is a direct randomized comparison, but it comes from one small cohort and one research group. A larger independent trial should confirm the result and assess whether pain relief persists and improves daily activity.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term pain reduction after varicocelectomy
Publications and records1 unique publication and cohort

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One 60-participant double-blind trial found lower pain and higher sexual-satisfaction scores after red or near-infrared laser than after sham during its short follow-up. The randomized comparison supports a short-term effect, but it is a single-center study from one research group. Independent replication and follow-up for recurrence, function, and adverse effects would support a stronger rating.
